analysis.one_liner: Overrides endangered-species pumping limits in California's Bay-Delta to send more water to San Joaquin Valley farms.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by Rep. Jim Costa with one cosponsor, was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, never received a vote, and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have declared that the federal projects pumping water out of California's Bay-Delta were fully complying with the Endangered Species Act, as long as they followed fixed flow and pumping rules written into the bill. That would loosen the pumping restrictions that cut water deliveries to San Joaquin Valley farms, and it would bar California from enforcing anything stricter. In exchange, it ordered a delta smelt hatchery and habitat-restoration projects, and it expired on March 1, 2015.
analysis.who_benefits: Westside San Joaquin Valley farmers and irrigation districts, and other contractors of the federal Central Valley Project and California State Water Project, would receive more exported water in most years. Farm towns in the valley that depend on fieldwork and packing jobs would share in that gain, and the bill's savings clause guarantees no cut in State Water Project deliveries, which serve urban Southern California as well.
analysis.who_benefits_short: San Joaquin Valley farms and water districts

how_it_helps.text: Declares Endangered Species Act requirements for the Central Valley Project and State Water Project satisfied once the government scientists' 'Reasonable and Prudent Alternatives' are implemented alongside the bill's own pumping mandates — including a floor on reverse flows in Old and Middle Rivers from December through June and limits on export reductions in April and May — lifting the operational restrictions that had cut deliveries.

Softens the fall 'X2' salinity standard, requiring it only to the extent it does not reduce either project's ability to deliver water for other purposes, and preempts any California state law that would restrict the projects more than the bill does.

Adds substitute conservation measures: a delta smelt hatchery or refuge run with the governor, a habitat and fish-passage program for the Bay-Delta and its tributaries, and installation of the Head of Old River Barrier during the April–May pulse flow.

Includes a one-way safety valve for water users: the Interior Secretary may modify the pumping mandates only if the change helps the species AND does not reduce water delivery capability, so science could loosen the rules but never tighten them; the whole scheme sunsets March 1, 2015.

analysis.who_pays: The Bay-Delta ecosystem and the fish protected under the biological opinions, chiefly delta smelt and salmon runs, would bear the cost: fixed pumping mandates would replace the scientists' ability to adjust operations as conditions change. Commercial and recreational salmon fisheries, which depend on healthy runs, would bear much of that loss, and California would lose its authority to set stricter rules for water projects inside its own borders.
analysis.who_pays_short: Bay-Delta fish, salmon fisheries, California's authority

drawbacks.text: 'Deemed satisfied' compliance means federal wildlife biologists would no longer be able to adjust pumping to protect fish when conditions demand it — the bill's mandates override the biological opinions even when circumstances change, which could push delta smelt and salmon runs closer to extinction.

The modification clause is a one-way ratchet: the Secretary can relax pumping limits if science supports it, but can never tighten them below the delivery capability set by the bill, no matter what the science shows.
Preempting stricter state law strips California of its usual role in managing water projects that operate entirely within its own borders and affect its own ecosystem.

Hatcheries and habitat projects are a substitute, not an equivalent: the bill trades in-delta flow protections — which keep fish away from the pumps — for hatchery production and restoration work whose benefits to species would be slower and less certain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver real, near-term water supply to valley agriculture and could ease hardship in farm towns with very high unemployment, which its findings describe in detail. But it buys that supply by replacing biologists' adaptive management with fixed pumping rules, making the science effectively powerless to tighten protections, and by overriding state law. The conservation measures it offers in return are speculative compared to the flow protections being traded away. It was a lopsided bargain weighted toward the largest water users.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Costa, joined by Rep. Dennis Cardoza as original cosponsor, introduced the bill on March 30, 2011, framing it as relief for a valley where 400,000 acres had been fallowed in 2009 and rural unemployment was near 40 percent.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources — the only committee referral it ever received.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote followed; the bill's action history ends with the referral, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Bay-Delta ecosystem, the fish listed under the biological opinions, and the salmon fisheries that depend on them are better off, because the pumping limits stayed in place and California's authority to regulate the projects was never overridden. Valley water users gained nothing from the bill's death.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were California Democrats and there was never a recorded vote; the Republican-controlled Natural Resources Committee simply took no action, so the party split, if any, was never tested.

industries.industry: San Joaquin Valley westside agriculture and irrigation districts
industries.note: The bill's core purpose was restoring water deliveries cut by the biological opinions, and the largest contract holders are big farming operations. Farm jobs and valley towns would have shared the benefit, but the water would come at the expense of a public resource — the delta ecosystem and its protected species.

Relaxing Old and Middle River flow limits and April–May export caps would draw more migrating salmon toward the export pumps, and salmon losses translate directly into lost fishing seasons and income — the industry's loss is agriculture's gain.

industries.industry: Federal and State Water Project contractors, including Southern California urban agencies
industries.note: The bill's savings clause guarantees no reduction in State Water Project deliveries to its contractors, and loosened pumping restrictions increase supply reliability for both farm and urban customers south of the delta.

industries.industry: Delta smelt and listed-fish hatchery and restoration contractors
industries.note: The bill mandates a smelt hatchery program, habitat restoration, and fish passage projects, directing federal spending toward ecosystem work even as it relaxes flow protections.
